title: Bode gain-phase relations and minimum-phase systems

sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 186" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>Magnitude slope in two regions, the clue a minimum-phase phase curve follows</title><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="300" y2="156"/><polygon points="300,156 293.6,158.7 293.6,153.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="50" y2="30"/><polygon points="50,30 52.7,36.4 47.3,36.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="300" y="172" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">log ω</text><text x="54" y="26" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">|H| dB</text><polyline points="58,42 150,86 268,142" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="96" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−20</text><text x="188" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−40</text></svg>
sections.figure_alt: A magnitude curve with a gentle negative slope, then a steeper one. Slope labels are -20 and -40. No phase curve is drawn.
sections.body_md:
On a minimum-phase frequency response, the magnitude slope and the phase are tied together. A slope of \(-20\ \mathrm{dB}\) per decade, held across a wide band, sits near \(-90^\circ\). A slope of \(-40\ \mathrm{dB}\) per decade sits near \(-180^\circ\), and \(-60\) near \(-270^\circ\). The phase at one frequency is a weighted average of the slope nearby, so a slope that has only just changed has not yet dragged the phase all the way to the new value.

A system is minimum phase when every zero is in the open left half-plane and there is no time delay. Among stable systems with the same magnitude curve, it has the smallest phase lag. A right-half-plane zero matches the magnitude of its left-half-plane mirror and contributes the opposite phase, toward \(-90^\circ\) instead of \(+90^\circ\). The ratio of those two factors is an all-pass of magnitude \(1\). A delay \(e^{-sT}\) also has magnitude \(1\) and adds lag \(\omega T\) radians. Both eat phase margin as the bandwidth goes up.

A right-half-plane zero shows up in time as well. The step response first moves the wrong way, then settles in the commanded direction. That initial reversal is inverse response.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Wideband slope of \(-20n\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) implies phase near \(-90n\) degrees, for a minimum-phase response.
\[ \frac{z-s}{z+s}\ \text{on}\ s = j\omega \quad\text{has magnitude}\ 1\ \text{and phase}\ -2\tan^{-1}(\omega/z). \]
A delay of \(T\) seconds has phase \(-\omega T\) radians. The gap between a right-half-plane zero and its left-half-plane mirror, at the frequency \(\omega = z\), is \(90^\circ\) of extra lag.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(H(s) = (10 - s)/(s + 4)\) at \(\omega = 7\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The numerator magnitude is \(\sqrt{10^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{149}\) and the denominator magnitude is \(\sqrt{4^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{65}\), so \(|H| = 1.514\). The numerator angle is \(\tan^{-1}(-7/10)\) and the denominator angle is \(\tan^{-1}(7/4)\).

Compare the right-half-plane zero with a left-half-plane zero at \(-10\). The mirror would have contributed \(+\tan^{-1}(7/10)\) instead of \(-\tan^{-1}(7/10)\). The difference is the all-pass phase \(-2\tan^{-1}(7/10) = -69.98^\circ\). A separate \(12\ \mathrm{ms}\) delay at \(25\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) adds another \(0.3\) radian, which is \(17.19^\circ\), with no change in magnitude.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Reading phase off the magnitude slope when the system has a right-half-plane zero or a delay. The slope rule is only for minimum-phase systems.
- Treating a right-half-plane zero as an unstable pole. Poles in the right half-plane make the free response grow. Zeros there do not, by themselves.
- Swapping the sign of the zero's phase. Left-half-plane zeros lead. Right-half-plane zeros lag.
- Expecting the phase to jump the instant the magnitude slope changes. The phase moves gradually, over about a decade on either side of a corner.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Feedback runs into this tie as a design limit. An right-half-plane zero or a delay adds lag that no magnitude shaping can remove. Crossover has to stay well below that zero, and well below \(1/T\) for a delay, if phase margin is still required. A steeper loop slope near crossover costs the same margin, which is why loop shaping and the waterbed constraint are the next questions.
